title: Why is std::unordered_map losing to a sorted vector on 200k lookups?
author: segfaulter

replies.author: midnight_compiler
replies.body:
Your guess is right and 3x is normal. The standard basically mandates a bad layout: `unordered_map` is required to have stable references and bucket iteration, which forces separate chaining with individually allocated nodes. Every single lookup is at minimum one miss on the bucket array and one on the node.

Two other things eating you:

1. `m[k]` is not a lookup, it's an insert-if-missing. It has to be non-const and it can rehash. Use `m.find(k)` if you're only reading.
2. The default hash for `int` in libstdc++ is identity. If your keys have any structure you get clustering for free.

If you want a real hash map, `absl::flat_hash_map` or `ankerl::unordered_dense` are open-addressed and usually beat the sorted vector back.

replies.author: off_by_one
replies.body:
Also: if the keys are known up front and you never insert after, the sorted vector is just the correct data structure. "Hash map for lookups" is a reflex, not a rule.

The crossover in my testing is somewhere around a few thousand elements *if* you're doing mixed insert/lookup. Read-only, the vector wins basically forever.

replies.author: nandhole
replies.body: worth timing the sort separately btw. if you're paying 80ms to sort so you can save 220ms on lookups that's still a win here, but it flips if you only do a handful of lookups.
